section_title: What does it mean to come to the bread of life?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 35 Jesus answered, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.

context_lines: After the crowd asks for the true bread from heaven, Jesus identifies Himself as the bread of life. Coming to Him and believing in Him appear together as the response to His gift.

The surrounding promise leads toward eternal life and resurrection, rather than a claim that believers never again need ordinary food or drink. [Read John 6:35–40 in context](https://the-way-of-scripture.web.app/passages/john-6-35-40.html).
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readers agree that Jesus promises to welcome those who come to Him and to give believers life and resurrection. Where traditions differ is how the Father’s giving and the believer’s continuing faith fit together.

Reformed teaching in the Westminster Confession says that God brings those He has chosen to Christ, makes them willing to come, and preserves them to the end. Calvin reads these verses as an assurance that none whom the Father gives to the Son will finally be lost. ([Westminster Confession 10.1–2; 17.1–3](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html); [Calvin on John 6:37–39](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/john/6.htm))

Wesley reads the promises with the condition of continuing in faith to the end. Catholic teaching likewise describes faith as God’s free gift, while teaching that it can be lost and must be nourished through a life of faith and love. These broader teachings help explain why their readers do not take the promise as removing the call to persevere. ([Wesley on John 6:37–40](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/); [Catechism §162](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.index.html))
god_plan_lines: Paul describes Christ’s resurrection as the beginning of the harvest for those who belong to Him. Those who are His will be raised at His coming. The promise here rests within that larger victory over death, made certain by the Son’s own resurrection. ([1 Corinthians 15:20–23](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm))

The same passage looks ahead to the defeat of death as the last enemy and the completion of Christ’s reign under the Father. Raising believers is therefore part of God’s purpose to overcome death and bring His rule to completion. ([1 Corinthians 15:24–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/15.htm))
current_position_lines: Our study Prayer and Faith reads the true bread from heaven as Christ Himself, whom the Father gives for life. It connects this passage with daily dependence on Him as the source of lasting life, rather than treating bread only as material provision.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Prayer and Faith: Section4 The Missing Link — Christ as the Living Bread; developed John6:32–58 discussion and quoted32–33/35/48–51/58. Limited to identity of bread/faith/dependence, without originating a Eucharistic or election position.
